title: Looking back: year five
hookLine: the sources, the perfections, the householder, death, the life of practice
tomorrow: what's the second arrow, and who shoots it?

cards: A grandparent's voice memo can land harder than any photo: the pauses, the accent, the laugh in the middle of a sentence. This year you read the sources: the perfections, the householder, death, a life of practice.
Open almost any of those discourses and the first words aren't the Buddha's. They're a listener's. Thus have I heard.
In Pali, evam me sutam. Why would the core texts of a tradition open by admitting they're secondhand? The answer is a sound, not a page.

teach.b: Tradition says that after the Buddha died, the monks gathered to agree on what he had taught, and Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, who had walked beside him and heard so much, recited the discourses.
Each one he began the same way: thus have I heard, at one time the Blessed One was staying at such a place. Not I say. I heard.
The words passed from voice to ear, monks chanting them together so nothing slipped, long before they were written down.
Chanting has a feel: a low hum in the chest, many voices on one note, and a slip is easy to hear, because the room stops matching.
So the sources you read this year were sound before they were ink.

That's why Buddhists chant. At a temple, at a funeral, at a house blessing, monks and lay people still chant suttas aloud, often in Pali, the way the words first traveled. The opening is also a small lesson in humility.
Even Ananda didn't claim the teaching as his. He only promised to pass it on as he heard it. And that's what you did all year.
The sources came to you secondhand, through many voices, and you heard them.

how: Monks and lay Buddhists chant suttas aloud at temples, funerals, house blessings and daily services, in Pali in Theravada communities and in other languages elsewhere; a sutta traditionally opens 'thus have I heard'.

o: reading the newest teachers instead of the older ones
turning to a past year of the path to see what it gave

games.q: your friend says a teaching that was passed on by memory for generations can't be trusted. what does the opening line of a sutta say back?
o: it doesn't claim more than it is: 'thus have I heard', from a listener, chanted together so nothing slipped.
nothing; the suttas were dictated word for word and never passed by memory.
she's right; anything heard rather than written should be thrown out.
games.why: the sutta itself names the chain: heard, then passed on. tradition says monks chanted together to keep the words whole.

practice: Find the quietest steady sound around you: a fan, a fridge, rain, your own breath. Listen to it the whole way through the sit, the way Ananda's listeners listened, with nothing to add.
At the end, if you like, say softly the words every sutta hands down: evam me sutam, thus have I heard.

wordCard.voice: Looking back, at year five: the sources, which reached you the way they reached everyone, as something heard.

carryVoice: Your line: the sources, heard before they were read. Five years looked back on, one day at a time.
